title: Wives, Husbands, and Suffering for Doing Good
summary: Peter instructs wives, especially those with unbelieving husbands, to win them by pure conduct and inner beauty, and husbands to honor their wives as fellow heirs of the grace of life. He calls all believers to unity and compassion and to repay insult with blessing. Those who suffer for doing right are blessed, should be ready to explain their hope with gentleness, and can take courage from Christ, who suffered once for sins, was made alive, proclaimed to the spirits in prison, and now reigns at God's right hand.
story: Chapter 2 began a set of instructions for living among unbelievers: citizens and rulers, servants and masters. Chapter 3 continues that household code with wives and husbands and then widens to the whole church. From verse 13 on, the letter's theme of suffering for doing good comes to the center, and Peter grounds it in the story of Christ's death, resurrection, and ascension, reaching all the way back to Noah and the flood. The chapter's closing passage (verses 18-22) is one of the most debated in the New Testament, but its purpose in the letter is clear: the Christ who suffered now rules over every power, and those who belong to him share in his victory.
historical:
In the Roman world a wife was expected to share her husband's religion. The Greek moralist Plutarch, writing around the end of the first century, advised that a wife should worship only her husband's gods and shut the door to foreign cults. A woman who became a Christian while her husband remained pagan was therefore in a vulnerable and suspicious position, seen as disloyal to her household. Peter addresses exactly this situation: he does not tell her to abandon her faith, which would be the social expectation, but to live it out in a way that might win her husband without words.

The verses about Noah assume familiarity with Genesis 6-9, and probably with Jewish traditions built on Genesis 6:1-4, where the sons of God took human wives before the flood. In the book of 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing from the last centuries BC that was widely read in the first century, these sons of God were rebellious angels, the Watchers, who were imprisoned in punishment. The same tradition stands behind 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6. Whether Peter draws on it is part of the debate over verse 19.
cultural:
Outward adornment was a mark of status in Roman society, and elaborate braided hairstyles with gold ornaments were fashionable among wealthy women. Moralists, pagan and Jewish, often criticized such display. Peter commends instead the “unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit”, and his example is Sarah, who called Abraham lord (compare Genesis 18:12), a term of respect for a husband in that culture. The description of wives as “a delicate vessel” probably refers to physical strength and to women's weaker legal and social position; in the same breath Peter calls them “fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life”, equal before God, and warns husbands that dishonoring their wives will hinder their prayers.

Christians today disagree about how these instructions apply to marriage. Complementarian readers hold that the call to wives reflects an enduring pattern of loving headship and willing submission within marriage. Egalitarian readers hold that Peter adapts the household code of his culture for the sake of mission, and that the gospel's deeper principle is mutual submission and shared inheritance. Both agree the passage never licenses a husband's harshness or abuse. Submission in this passage is never a duty to accept violence or cruelty, and anyone in an abusive marriage should seek safety and help from trusted people, a pastor or counselor, or the authorities.
literary: Verses 1-7 complete the household code begun in 2:13, with the repeated phrase “in the same way” linking wives and husbands to the example of Christ in 2:21-25. Verse 8 opens with “Finally” and gives a summary list of virtues for all, followed by a quotation of Psalm 34:12-16 that frames the rest of the chapter: the Lord watches over the righteous. Verses 13-17 turn to suffering, quoting Isaiah 8:12-13. Verses 18-22 are a compact, almost creedal passage that many scholars think draws on early Christian hymns or confessions. It moves in a sequence (suffered, put to death, made alive, went, preached, raised, gone into heaven, at the right hand) that traces Christ's path from the cross to his throne. The verb for went (poreutheis) appears in verse 19 and again in verse 22 (“has gone into heaven”), a detail important for interpreting the passage.

outline.t: Wives and the witness of conduct
Husbands and honor for fellow heirs
Unity, compassion, and blessing for insult
Suffering for doing good and a ready defense

doctrines.note: “Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.” The death is unrepeatable, substitutionary, and reconciling; its aim is to bring people to God.

Baptism “now saves you” not as outward washing but as “the pledge of a clear conscience toward God” through Christ's resurrection. Traditions that see baptism as a means of grace emphasize the first phrase; traditions that see it as a sign of faith emphasize the second. All agree its power comes from the risen Christ, not the water.

Peter addresses wives and husbands as fellow heirs of grace, calling for conduct that honors God, respects the other, and bears witness to unbelievers. Christians differ on how the specific instructions apply, but not on the equal dignity of husband and wife before God.
Suffering for what is right is a blessing, not a defeat, because Christ also suffered and was vindicated. “It is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.”

words.note: Apologia, a defense, such as a speech given in a law court (compare Acts 25:16), and the root of the English apologetics. Peter wants every believer ready to give a reasoned account of their hope to anyone who asks, whether an official or a curious neighbor, with gentleness and respect.

Kērussō, to proclaim or herald, the announcement of a message by an authorized messenger. It usually refers to preaching the gospel, but it can mean announcing any news, including victory or judgment. Whether Christ's proclamation in verse 19 offered salvation or announced triumph depends on which reading of the passage one follows.

Phulakē, prison, guard, or watch. It describes a place of confinement. The spirits in prison are those held in custody, whether understood as fallen angels awaiting judgment or as the dead of Noah's generation.

Eperōtēma, rendered “pledge” in verse 21. The word can mean a question, a request, or a formal answer or commitment given in response to a question, and interpreters debate whether baptism is an appeal to God for a clean conscience or a pledge made to God from one. Some connect it with questions asked of candidates at baptism.

christ: Verses 18-22 give one of the fullest summaries of Christ's work anywhere in the New Testament. He suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring people to God. He was put to death in the body and made alive in the Spirit. He proclaimed his message to the spirits in prison. He rose, and through his resurrection baptism saves. He has gone into heaven and sits at God's right hand, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to him, fulfilling Psalm 110:1. Peter sets this story before readers who suffer for doing good so that they see where their path leads: the one they follow went through death to a throne. The command to “sanctify Christ as Lord” in their hearts (verse 15) applies to Jesus the words Isaiah 8:13 used of the LORD himself, a quiet confession of his deity.

hard.q: Who are the spirits in prison, and what did Christ preach to them (verses 19-20)?
hard.a:
This is one of the most disputed passages in the New Testament, and the church has read it in several ways. The first reading, held by Augustine, is that the preexistent Christ, in the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day, who refused to repent and are now in prison awaiting judgment. It fits Peter's description of Noah's generation and avoids any idea of a second chance after death, but it takes went in an unusual sense.

A second reading holds that between his death and resurrection Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached to the souls there. Some early Christian writers understood this as an offer of salvation to those who died before his coming, others as the release of Old Testament believers (the harrowing of hell in later tradition), and others as a proclamation of judgment. This reading has shaped the clause of the Apostles' Creed that Christ descended to the dead, a clause that entered the creed over time, and Christians connect it also with 1 Peter 4:6. Some take the passage as evidence of hope for those who never heard; most who hold this reading limit it to what Peter says.

A third reading, favored by many modern commentators, holds that the spirits are fallen angels imprisoned for their rebellion in Noah's day (Genesis 6:1-4, as read in 1 Enoch; compare 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), and that the risen Christ, on his way to heaven (the same verb went in verse 22), announced his victory over them. This fits the New Testament's usual use of spirits for nonhuman beings and the passage's climax, with powers subject to him.

All three readings agree on the point Peter is making: Christ's suffering led to triumph over every opposing power, and those who suffer with him will share it.

questions: Peter hopes that conduct will win people who do not believe the word. What in your daily conduct speaks, for good or ill, to the people closest to you?
How would you explain, briefly and with gentleness and respect, the reason for the hope that is in you?
What difference does it make to your fears that Christ now reigns with angels, authorities, and powers subject to him?
